approaches.name: Pure Resource-Oriented REST with Flat Paths
approaches.summary: All resources are top-level nouns (/orders, /carts, /return-requests, /payments, /skus, etc.). State transitions are expressed purely via PATCH with a 'status' field. Filtering, sorting, and pagination use a consistent query-string convention (?filter[brand]=X&filter[price_min]=Y&sort=-created_at&page=1&limit=20). No action sub-resources; all mutations go through standard HTTP verbs on the resource itself.
pros: Maximum uniformity — every resource follows the same CRUD shape, making the API easy to document with OpenAPI and easy for frontend developers to learn
Flat paths avoid deep nesting ambiguity (e.g. no question of whether cart items live under /carts/:id/items or /cart-items)
Stateless PATCH-based status updates are simple to implement with Express route handlers
Cache-friendly: GET /products, GET /skus, GET /categories all cache cleanly at CDN or reverse-proxy level
cons: State-machine transitions (cancel order, approve return, advance fulfilment stage) are semantically ambiguous as plain PATCHes — nothing in the URL or verb signals intent, making access control rules and audit logging harder to attach

Business side-effects (release stock on cancel, trigger refund on return approval) must be inferred from the status field change server-side, coupling transition logic invisibly to a generic update handler
Guest checkout session management and multi-step checkout state are awkward to express as resource PATCHes without inventing a checkout-session resource anyway
Promo code validation and PIN serviceability checks are not natural CRUDs but become forced GETs with query params, losing clarity

approaches.name: Hybrid REST + Action Sub-Resources
approaches.summary: Core CRUD entities use standard REST nouns and HTTP verbs with shallow nesting where ownership is clear (GET /orders/:id/items, GET /users/:id/addresses). State-machine transitions that carry side-effects are modelled as POST action sub-resources: POST /orders/:id/cancel, POST /orders/:id/advance-status, POST /return-requests/:id/approve, POST /return-requests/:id/reject. Stateless lookups like PIN serviceability and promo validation are RPC-style POSTs or GETs on dedicated sub-paths. Checkout is a dedicated resource (/checkouts) with step-scoped PATCHes (address, review, payment). Filtering uses bracketed query params; cursor-based pagination for order history/catalogue lists.
pros: Action sub-resources make side-effectful transitions explicit and self-documenting: POST /orders/:id/cancel clearly signals stock release and refund recording, making RBAC middleware and audit hooks trivial to attach at the route level
Staff 'advance status' flow (REQ-4) maps directly to POST /orders/:id/advance-status, isolating fulfilment logic from generic update logic
Returns two-step flow (REQ-6, REQ-7) maps cleanly: POST /orders/:id/return-requests (customer creates) → POST /return-requests/:id/approve (staff approves), each gated by role middleware

Checkout as a first-class resource (/checkouts/:id) naturally holds reservation TTL, promo discount, GST totals, and guest email — solving cart-preservation on payment failure (REQ-32) without hacking the cart resource
Shallow nesting (one level deep at most) keeps URLs readable while still expressing ownership; flat alternatives remain available for admin bulk queries
Promo validation (POST /promo-codes/validate) and PIN serviceability (GET /serviceable-pin-codes/:pin) are explicit, cacheable, and clearly named
Elasticsearch-backed search and faceted filters map cleanly to GET /products/search?q=&filter[brand]=&filter[price_max]=&sort=rating with aggregations returned alongside results
cons: More endpoint surface area than pure REST — developers need to know both the noun endpoints and the action endpoints
Requires disciplined convention enforcement (e.g. always POST for actions, never PATCH status directly) to avoid drift as the team grows

Shallow nesting means some cross-cutting admin queries (all return requests across all orders) need a flat /return-requests endpoint alongside the nested one, creating two canonical paths for the same resource

approaches.name: Command-Oriented RPC-Style API
approaches.summary: All mutations are named commands POSTed to a single /commands or feature-scoped action endpoints: POST /orders/commands/cancel, POST /orders/commands/advance, POST /cart/commands/add-item, POST /checkout/commands/apply-promo, POST /returns/commands/request, POST /returns/commands/approve. Reads are resource-oriented GETs. Inspired by CQRS: commands carry full intent and payload; queries return projections. Auth token claims are checked per command type.
pros: Perfect alignment with complex business rules — each command handler owns exactly one use-case including all side-effects, making the business logic layer explicit and independently testable
Eliminates ambiguity for state transitions entirely; no risk of a PATCH accidentally bypassing business rule checks
Scales naturally if the system later adopts an event-sourced or message-queue architecture for order fulfilment simulation
cons: Dramatically higher learning curve for frontend developers accustomed to REST — every mutation requires knowing the exact command name and payload shape
Read endpoints still need to be RESTful GETs, creating a mixed metaphor that adds cognitive overhead
OpenAPI documentation becomes verbose and non-standard; tooling like REST clients and API explorers offer less automatic help
Significant over-engineering for a Node.js + Express + MySQL build that has a small team and a tight launch scope; the operational complexity is not justified by catalogue scale or transaction volume

Guest checkout, cart, and catalogue CRUD (products, categories, brands, SKUs managed via admin CMS) are purely CRUD and gain nothing from the command pattern, so the approach is inconsistently applied across the app

decision.rationale: This app has a clear split between simple CRUD (catalogue, addresses, users, promo code management, notifications) and complex state-machine transitions with mandatory side-effects (order cancel → release stock; return approve → trigger refund; checkout start → reserve stock with TTL). Pure REST with PATCH-status conflates these two concerns and makes it hard to attach role guards and side-effect logic cleanly. Full CQRS/command-style is overkill for a Node+Express+MySQL monolith at this scale and team size. The hybrid approach gives uniform REST for catalogue, user, and admin CRUD — which maps directly to the admin CMS routes and Elasticsearch-backed product listing — while action sub-resources (POST /orders/:id/cancel, POST /orders/:id/advance-status, POST /return-requests/:id/approve) make every RBAC boundary explicit at the router level, keep side-effect logic isolated in named handlers, and directly satisfy REQ-2, REQ-4, REQ-6, REQ-9, and REQ-51 without ambiguity. The /checkouts resource handles multi-step checkout state, cart preservation on payment failure, guest email, GST calculation, and promo application in one cohesive place. Shallow one-level nesting (orders/:id/items, users/:id/addresses) expresses ownership without deep path complexity. This is the industry-proven pattern for e-commerce APIs of this complexity level and fits naturally with Express router composition and JWT-claim-based middleware.
